claims.text: The dynamic mechanical response of Co-free FeNiCrMn is primarily governed by a transition between dislocation-glide-dominated and deformation-twinning-dominated plasticity.
At high temperatures and/or low strain rates, FeNiCrMn deforms mainly by thermally activated dislocation glide.
At low temperatures and/or high strain rates, deformation twinning becomes the dominant plasticity mode in FeNiCrMn.
The transition between dislocation glide and deformation twinning controls the strength–ductility balance.
The relevant initial material is solidified, equiaxed-grained FeNiCrMn with a typical dendritic or cast microstructure.
The initial FeNiCrMn material has minimal pre-existing defects.
The presence and evolution of deformation twins and twin boundaries modulate strain-hardening capacity.
At high temperatures or low strain rates, increased thermal activation permits dislocation glide and dynamic recovery.
Dislocation glide and dynamic recovery at high temperatures or low strain rates produce lower yield strength and higher ductility.
At low temperatures or high strain rates, reduced dislocation mobility and limited recovery favor deformation twinning.
Twinning at low temperatures or high strain rates raises yield strength and reduces ductility.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate specimens will contain more clearly observable deformation twins than high-temperature, low-strain-rate specimens.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi has a different balance between dislocation-mediated and twinning-mediated deformation because it contains Co.
The proposed mechanism applies only in temperature regimes that avoid phase transformations and recrystallization.
The proposed mechanism applies only at strain rates for which adiabatic shear does not dominate.
Ultra-high strain rates that cause substantial heating may activate additional mechanisms.
